title: Taking out: cold MoE experts moved to router-ahead prefetched DDR4 tier
idea: TRIZ #2 Taking out the cold mass: mixture-of-experts models keep only routed-hot experts in HBM, and the rest live in commodity DDR4 behind 28 nm CXL controllers. A tiny predictor runs the next layer's router one layer early so the needed experts stream over CXL before they are used. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Do DRAM's job with less HBM: 2-4x less HBM per accelerator for MoE inference, shifting capacity to cheap trailing-node DRAM.

title: Index-list gather engine returns only packed useful words
idea: Ideal: the memory already knows which words you need. Closest achievable: the host sends a list of 4-8 byte indices (embedding rows, sparse nonzeros, KV pages) over the command path, and the base die does bank-parallel fetches and returns densely packed 64 B lines holding only the requested words.
why: Fact 8 and fact 5: sparse and embedding workloads waste 80-95% of transferred bytes; packing cuts interface traffic 5-10x for those patterns.

title: Top-k memory: base die filters KV cache before the link
idea: Invert 'memory returns what was asked for': for attention, the host sends the query vector to the HBM base die, which scores keys in low precision across the KV pages beneath it and returns only the top-k keys/values at full precision.
why: Long-context decode is KV-bandwidth-bound; returning 5-10% of KV entries cuts link traffic 10-20x and lets longer contexts live in fewer, cheaper stacks.
note: 10-20x less KV link traffic in long-context decode; doubt: low-precision top-k accuracy, and attention-PIM is crowded art.

title: One optical copy of weights broadcast to a hundred accelerators
idea: First principles: read-only weights need O(1) storage, not O(N) copies, if broadcast bandwidth exists. Keep one model copy in a central memory node and stream it in layer order through a passive 1:128 optical splitter tree to accelerators running in lockstep; each holds only a few-layer SRAM ring buffer.
why: Weight GB per accelerator falls ~100x, so cost per served GB ~100x lower; trades scheduling flexibility (all nodes run the same layer at once).
note: One weight copy streamed to many lockstep accelerators; broadcast bandwidth, splitter loss and lockstep scheduling are doubts.

title: Copying: passive optical splitters broadcast one weight read to many chips
idea: TRIZ #26 Copying: in data-parallel inference every accelerator holds an identical copy of the weights. Instead, one memory node reads each weight block once and broadcasts it in lockstep to all accelerators through cheap passive 1:16 PON fiber splitters (mass-produced telecom parts). (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Do DRAM's job with less: replicated weight storage falls by up to 16x, freeing HBM for KV cache, using existing telecom optics capacity.
note: PON-class optics far below HBM bandwidth; only works for lockstep streaming.

title: Nanoimprinted oxide-TFT memory built into glass package substrates
idea: Display fabs process glass at ~$100-300/m^2 versus ~$70,000/m^2 for finished DRAM wafers, a ~300x area-cost gap. Use nanoimprint lithography at 40-50 nm half-pitch on Gen-8 panels to pattern oxide-TFT gain cells, then cut the panel into glass-core package substrates carrying the memory directly under the chiplets.
why: At ~1/3 DRAM density, cost per bit ~100x lower and U.S.-manufacturable in display/glass lines; trades speed, retention and density.
note: Doubt: 40 nm NIL overlay and IGZO variability on Gen-8 glass; display $/m2 won't hold at that resolution.

title: Twin synchronized predictors send only the surprise
idea: Information theory says only unpredicted bits must cross a channel. Run identical stride/context/value predictors on both sides of the memory link; the sender transmits a 1-bit hit flag when the receiver's prediction is right and an XOR residual otherwise, and both update identically so they stay in lockstep.
why: Regular pointers, zeros and strides could cut bits crossing the interface 2-5x, lowering link pJ and bandwidth demand (facts 5, 8).

title: Twenty-millivolt bitline-style die-to-die links bounded by kT/C
idea: The true floor on signal swing is thermal noise sqrt(kT/C), ~0.2 mV rms on a 100 fF bonded link, so 20 mV still gives >10 sigma margin. Replace 0.4 V HBM drivers with charge-dump transmitters and cross-coupled latch receivers clocked like a DRAM sense amp (precharge, share, regenerate), with per-lane offset trim stored at boot.
why: Energy ~C*VDD*dV falls ~20x versus 0.4 V swing: HBM 3-4 pJ/bit toward ~0.2 pJ/bit (fact 5), and smaller I/O cells shrink periphery (fact 7).

title: Bit-significance stack: MSB planes on clean dies, LSB planes on cheap dies
idea: Shift the unit of placement from the word to the bit-plane along the stack's vertical axis: sign, exponent and high-mantissa planes go to 4 protected dies, low-order planes go to 8 dies running at 1% BER with no ECC, and the base die re-interleaves planes into words on the fly.
why: Two-thirds of bits live on refresh-relaxed, low-voltage dies (facts 3, 10) with <0.1% model-quality loss; precision-on-demand fetching also cuts data moved up to ~50%.

title: Circulating drum memory: streaming access refreshes ultra-leaky cheap cells
idea: Capacitor size and leakage specs exist only to hold charge for 64 ms; if every row is read-and-restored every 100 us because data circulates through compute like a drum, retention can be 640x worse. That permits planar MIM capacitors on short bitlines and leaky access devices in fully depreciated 28-40 nm fabs, with no high-AR etch and no EUV, behind a controller that streams rows in fixed order.
why: Strips capital (~55% of wafer cost) and the capacitor/EUV steps; claimed 10-100x lower cost per GB with high uncertainty; trades random access for sequential revolution latency.
note: Sequential circulation replaces retention; mature-node planar cells limit density, so 10-100x cost claim is doubtful.

title: Stacked camera-sensor pixel bonding: per-subarray copper ports to logic
idea: Adapted from the pixel-level Cu-Cu hybrid bonding of stacked smartphone image sensors: the DRAM array wafer bonds face-to-face to a logic wafer so each subarray (mat) has its own ~100-wire vertical port. Global I/O routing and shared periphery go away.
why: Periphery 49% of die (fact 7) and data movement: array efficiency toward ~75% and >10x bandwidth at ~0.1 pJ/bit vertical hops.
note: Per-mat vertical ports remove global I/O; real physics, but needs a DRAM-logic wafer bonding partner.

title: Transfer-print thin memory membranes, then wire them lithographically
idea: Reverse bond-then-connect: undercut-release memory chiplets into <10 um membranes, pick them with a PDMS stamp onto the logic wafer, planarize with BCB, and pattern vias and copper across both with ordinary lithography, giving a monolithic-like 2-3 um-pitch connection with no bumps.
why: Fact 5: interconnect density ~10x microbumps at ~0.05 pJ/bit, using university-standard transfer printing, spin coating and plating.
